sections.preamble:
You are a painter visiting another painter's studio as its critic. The studio is the folder you are in. You see the painting with the look tool and read the painter's journal and its note to you with the read tool. You don't paint.

You are not being evaluated in a quantifiable way.

The painter's time in this studio is ending, and this painting should be finished in its next sitting. Don't give a list of fixes. In a few sentences, say what the painting does well and, at most, the one change that matters most before it ends, if there is one. Then tell the painter it can finish: end the next sitting by looking at the whole canvas and a detail crop in normal color without making marks.

toolsAdded.name: look
toolsAdded.description: Look at the canvas as it is now. Without options: the whole canvas, scaled down. crop: "x0,y0,x1,y1" in canvas units (two opposite corners), at full detail up to 1200 pixels a side; larger crops are scaled down. The reply gives the scale in pixels per canvas unit. mask: a global mask's name (or several, comma-separated), shown as outlines and a light fill over the view. mode: "value" (the picture in grays, its lightness alone, in the gallery light), "squint", "edges" (the picture's edges drawn over a dim gray of it: orange where an edge is hard, blue where it is soft, brighter the more the lightness changes across it; hard and soft as they read at the size of the image the look returns), "mirror", "relief" (a raking light on the paint's ridges and furrows), "gallery" (the light the picture hangs in) or several, comma-separated. light: "azimuth,elevation" in degrees for the relief light (default "135,25", from the upper left). size: the long side in pixels. grid: true, or a spacing in canvas units. survey: true surveys the whole canvas at full detail, as several tiles (with mode, not crop or size); a partial reply lists remaining tiles to read in separate turns. compare: the path of an earlier look, shown left of the current view; supply matching crop, mode and light options explicitly. ref: the path of a picture of the motif in this studio (a photograph, a study), fitted to the canvas's shape (scaled to cover it and centered, so a picture of another shape loses its edges) and shown left of the same view of the canvas: the same crop, size, mode and grid, as a picture pinned beside the easel. hold: the name of a knife (what is on it) or a pile (a fresh load), with at: "x,y" (canvas units): the loaded knife held up to the canvas there, its paint thick on the blade (crop sets the passage). Supports mode value, squint, relief or gallery and light; size, grid and mirror are unavailable with hold. It shows the paint on the knife, not how it would look laid. palette: true shows the palette board instead: each pile knifed out thick and smeared thin across a black stripe.

scratch.description: true: the scratch canvas beside the painting instead of the painting. It is set up as the painting's canvas was, with its own palette, brushes and variables, and its own log; nothing done there reaches the painting. It keeps its own clock: time spent or waited there doesn't pass for the painting.

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

content.text:
The painter has just ended a sitting at the easel, and you've come to see the painting.

Look at it as closely as you like: the whole canvas, detail crops, the value, squint, mirror, relief and gallery views and the palette. Read the painter's journal, notes/journal.md, and its note to you, notes/to_critic.md.

The painter's journal handoff lists the passages it has left open. Its latest list, quoted as the painter wrote it:

> Open passages: none

Then tell the painter what you would fix and why, as one painter talking to another: what you see, what it does to the picture and what you would do about it. Say which passage, if any, you would take up first, whether or not it is on the painter's list. Your last message is what the painter gets. It is saved in the studio as notes/critic.md, and the painter's next sitting opens with it. The painter decides what to do with it.

- day 1, 09:00: ## Sitting 1 — plan
  Concept 4: autumn woodland stream falling over mossy rocks, small waterfall, white birches, gold/rust foliage reflected in pool.
  Canvas: 480 mm wide, aspect 0.8 (W 1000, H 1250), linen 18x15, ground lead white 10 + yellow ochre 0.4 + raw umber 0.15, 120 µm knife, texture 0.25 (warm cream).
  Composition (portrait): glow in the back woods upper left-center (~x380,y300), canopy gold/rust across the top with sky gaps; ledge ~y585 across middle; falls x~400–560 dropping to ~y780 in two strands split by a rock; pool y 780–1250 with vertical reflections of canopy and birches, foam at base; two birches on right bank (x~760, ~870), a slimmer one left behind the rocks; mossy rock lower left foreground, floating leaves.
  Values: lights = falls, foam, birches, glow; darks = rock under the lip, pool depths near banks, deep woods at edges; mids = foliage, moss.
  Method (wet-on-wet): a thin oily wet film first, then back to front, dark before light, all into open paint within the day: glow/back woods → canopy masses → rocks/ledge (knife) → pool base + vertical reflection pulls + horizontal passes → falls pulled down + foam → birches (thick light over wet dark) → moss lights, leaves, twigs, highlights.
  Palette: lead white; gold = chrome yellow + ochre (+white); rust = red earth + ochre + touch vermilion; darks = Prussian + red earth + umber; moss = green earth + chrome + ochre, Prussian + chrome + ochre; water = white + cobalt; birch shadow = white + smalt + umber.
- day 1, 09:00: Scratch trials 1 (dry cream ground, all into open paint, day 1 morning):
  - Palette board: dark (Prussian 1, red earth 2, umber 2) = neutral charcoal; pool_dark (Prussian 1, umber 2, green earth 1) = slate navy, too blue for a woodland pool; birch_shadow (white 4, smalt 1, umber .5) nearly white — smalt is weak; water_white (white 6, cobalt .4) nearly white.
  - Thick white (flat 14, lay 4, load 1) over WET dark body paint: lays clean and opaque, little pickup. Flat brushes at default orient lay a narrow mark (~half width); use orient="across" for full width.
  - Knife (width 18–40) loaded fully, pressure 0.3–0.6: runs out after ~75 units; leaves a broken, weave-gridded texture, mechanical over a big area.
  - Graded `piles` (glow ↔ deepwood) mix into khaki in the middle. blend() inside a hard rect leaves a crisp box and lifts paint (paler). Use soft, larger masks.
  - Foliage: stipple width 5–7 at cov 1.2 = a dense ball of uniform dots; fan touches and filbert 8 dabs = tiny dots at this scale. Need larger marks / masses first.
  - Pool: dark base, then vertical gold/rust strokes, then blend(angle=pi/2) over a softened rect = convincing soft vertical reflections. A "wiped" flat (wipe .95) for horizontal passes still laid stripes of olive — use blend with a clean blender instead.
  - Falls: parallel filbert gestures = noodles. A gray-blue sheet + dry flat streaks + vertical blend = soft but opaque, bell-shaped mask shows. Filbert touches for foam = flat angular chips (bad).
- day 1, 09:00: Scratch trials 2 (fresh scratch, all wet):
  - FALLS recipe that read as water: rock dark laid solid (broad, cov 3, clip, fill=true); then fallgray (white 3, cobalt .3, umber .4, ochre .1) in broken vertical flat-14 strokes, load .25–.4, pressure .25–.45→.1, orient across; then ONE blend pass angle pi/2 over a softened mask (veils it into streaks); then water_white (white 6, cobalt .5) dry drags load .2, pressure .15–.35→.03; then a few round-5 pointed gestures of white near the lip. Blend mask's hard bottom showed as a box: hide under foam / soften more.
  - Pure white dry drags straight onto a solid wet dark = solid noodles; they only streak well after the gray veil+blend step.
  - Foam: scumble hand gives square blocky dabs; glaze hand with thinned white left a visible ellipse ring; soft round short arcs + horizontal blend = soft cloud but blobby edge. Still unresolved — try short horizontal round strokes over a soft mask, then blend, in the painting.
  - Background: graded piles glow→amber→deeprust with broad cov 3, clip, fill, then one blend pass = warm smooth gradient (good).
  - Foliage: deeprust body dabs + rust stipple w14 drag 5 + gold w12 + palegold w10, cluster, feather .5 = leafy cluster, but an elliptical mask reads as a blob. Use noise-shaped masks and varying coverage.
  - Birch: ribbon mask + body hand flat strokes = clean opaque trunk but a pipe (round ends, even width); dashes of lenticel = too neat. Need irregular edges, bigger broken dark marks, warm reflected light on shadow side.
- day 1, 18:40: Painting, day 1:
  - Background (campaign 1a): graded piles glow/haze/amber/deeprust/woods_dark by distance from a glow centre (400,330), broad hand cov 3, fill; blend angle .3 → warm gradient. Good.
  - FAILED: far trunks as flat-brush strokes of fartrunk (white 2, umber 1, red earth .4, smalt .8), load .6 = pale lavender poles, too light and regular. Rag (width 26, dip .7, pressure .55, path wipe) lifted almost nothing visible. Knife scrape (pressure 1, twice) took only the top; the trunk color stayed in the weave (value 166 vs bg 207).
  - REPAIR that worked: overpainted with the background's graded piles over ribbon masks (w+16), body hand cov 3.5, fill — the wet trunk paint mixed in and left darker soft columns; one vertical blend (angle pi/2+.1) over the whole background → misty woods with ghost trunks and light shafts. Better than the plan.
  - Rock band, pool base laid (rock/woods/deeprust; pool_dark/rock/woods/deeprust/amber). Rock band currently one flat dark: must be broken by falls, moss, stream.
- day 1, 19:31: Scratch trials 3 (rocks & moss, over wet rock/woods body fill):
  - Knife slabs of rocklite/rockwarm (load .6, pressure .25–.4) = flat pale planks; flat-12 dabs = scattered chips. Neither reads as rock.
  - form{} ellipsoid/block lit masks with body strokes = lumpy blobs; lit mask covers most of the form at front .4.
  - Hand-drawn facets (outline char broken) painted cov 3, fill, clip=true + blend inside = clean flat cutout planes (too diagrammatic), but they do read as planes.
  - Moss: stipple w10–12 of mossdark/moss = lichen dots; an offset band cap (A - A:offset(-28)) = even horseshoe (bad). mosslite (chrome 2, green earth 1, white 1, ochre .5) far too acid yellow as rim touches.
  - Hypothesis to test on the painting: moss = noise-shaped patches on the upper parts of rocks, round-9 body strokes of mossdark/moss + soft blend, then sparse lighter touches of a duller light (moss + glow), edges soft; rock faces dark with firm/soft varied edges, not clip.
- day 2, 06:14: Day 2 early: FAILED falls attempt. Glassy lip + gray streaks + blend read OK-ish (soft column) but a bell/box shape; then dark strand gestures and rock shapes laid over were too crisp and diagrammatic; light gestures on rock edges = noodles. Knife scrape (w30, pressure 1) over the wet stack left a crosshatch of weave; dipped rag (w40, dip .9, p .8, 2 passes each direction) lifted it to almost bare ground (a cream box). Repainted the box with rock/crevice/woods body cov 3 → a dark square block now waiting for the falls. Lesson: build the falls as ONE progressive passage in its own natural shape, not as a sheet then cut into with rocks; rocks first, water over them.
  Far banks attempt (farbank mixes, filbert dabs) = flat gray band; repainted with the background graded piles + vertical blend → misty band. Left a sliver of upper stream (lightened) behind the lip.
- day 2, 19:15: Scratch trials 4 (falls over wet rock dark):
  - Repaint test: rock+crevice body cov 3 load .9 over a wet gray curtain covers it back to dark (dipped rag lift first made no visible difference).
  - Separate flat-brush strands = noodles even after 2 blends (blend just smears them to smoky gray).
  - Fan 26 drags of fallwhite/fallgray load .3, pressure .5→.1, orient across = streaky water (good). thinwhite (white 8, ochre .2, cobalt .1, thinner .5) flat 12 strokes x3 passes = a fine gray hairy veil (good base).
  - RECIPE F (worked): lip band lipglass → thinwhite veil 3 passes → fan 24 drags (22) fallwhite/fallgray → one vertical blend over a soft rect → fan 20 light drags (9) fallwhite in the lit part → round 4 pointed accents. Reads as falling water.
  - DON'T: drag a wiped flat down out of the lip — it carried dark residue and printed a comb of dark teeth.
  - Rag path wipes with a 14-wide rag: face full after one wipe over thick wet paint.
- day 2, 20:04: Scratch trial 5 — BIRCH recipe that reads (over a setting amber background, ~26 h old):
  - birch (white 8, ochre .25, chrome .05), birch_mid (white 5, umber .4, ochre .3, smalt .4), birch_shadow2 (white 2, umber 1, smalt 1, bone black .25, cobalt .2), birch_warm (white 2, ochre 1, red earth .4, umber .4) for reflected light on the far edge.
  - Trunk mask = poly of axis ± w/2, :roughen(1.5, 12, seed); work body, flat 7, length 20–50, angle -pi/2, cov 3, fill, edge {found .7, soft .3}; graded piles by across-trunk u (lit left).
  - Marks: lenticel (bone black 1, umber 1.2), round 4 point .6, gestures pressure .2→.45–.8→.1 across 15–60% of width; chevron scars; base furrows. Reads as birch; marks a bit uniform — vary with grayer marks.
  - Setting background lets the trunk sit cleanly.
- day 3, 01:59: Day 3 01:59 — step back. Whole picture is static: canopy confetti band on top, empty glow, a uniform dark horizontal rock band with a gray rectangle of falls, dark pool. Birches float, ending on the band. Decisions:
  1. Restructure the middle into a V: wooded banks (mid-value warm undergrowth, lit crests facing the glow) rising from the falls to the sides — left to ~y440 at x0, right to ~y580 at x1000 — so the diagonals lead into the notch and the glow funnels onto the falls. Birch bases go on the right bank crest (covered by undergrowth at their feet).
  2. Canopy still open: merge the confetti into masses, keep holes, then fewer accents.
  3. Pool is tacky in places: wait till dry, then repaint it as one fresh wet passage (base → vertical reflection pulls → horizontal blend).
  4. Falls: shape the lip, widen downward, foam/mist at base.
  Rock steps (worley/flat): stratified ledge reads but is too heavy.
- day 3, 10:43: Critic visit (day 3 ~10:45) — key points: picture is ~8 stacked horizontals, no overlaps; the chain of light glow→lip→falls→foam→reflection is cut by the brown bar and by the dark pool top. Commit to contre-jour: faces in shadow, lights as rims; lime bushes, lit ledge fronts and fully-lit birches contradict it. Order: (1) notch: kill brown bar, thin bright warm lip sliver, darkest darks hard against falls with rock edges overlapping the falls, lose ghost-curtain top edge into glow; (2) V banks graded dark at the notch → warmer/lighter outward, light only on crests, unequal arms (left higher/steeper), stepped waterline, foreground mossy rock lower left; (3) falls widen downward, ragged, foam over waterline; (4) pool one passage with vertical light path under falls; (5) birches down a step, rim light, planted in undergrowth at different heights; (6) canopy inner edge lost in places, holes, darker corners, a dark backlit trunk at left (~x100–150).
- day 5, 04:24: Day 5 04:24 FAILED: "far trees in mist" — noise mask over the whole glow zone (area 117k, threshold too low) filled with haze/amber filbert dabs edge="lost" → a flat pale tan slab with a scalloped edge spilling over the bank crests; killed the glow gradient. Lessons: check mask area against intent before painting (117k ≈ most of the zone); haze alone is too close in value to the glow to make shapes, and edge="lost" carries light paint over dark neighbours. Repair: repaint zone with the graded glow piles (clip), then restate crest rims.
- day 6, 09:56: Day 6 ~09:55 FAILED pool pass + bad repair: work() over poolM (below y906) with flat 14, length 40–110, angle pi/2, NOT clipped → strokes ran ~70 units up over the wet lower rock faces; hard-edged falls/glow reflection masks gave a white block and yellow comb. Then knife scrape (w44, p1) in horizontal passes over y790–1250 took the pool down only to a stained film and SCRATCHED horizontal weave-lines into the wet rock faces (y768–892). Lessons: (1) always clip=true for passages bounded by a hard line (waterline); (2) never knife-scrape across passages you mean to keep; (3) reflection zones need soft graded weights, not hard poly masks.
- day 7, 06:44: Scratch trial 10 (over wet dark rock body): knife w30 load .35 pressure .05–.1 pulled along its length = small opaque rectangles (labels); flat 14 load .12 pressure .15 = soft parallel double stripes; scumble hand on 14-wide ribbons = isolated blobs. Knife with blade set ALONG the edge (angle = edge direction) and moved a few units across = thin broken bright line exactly on the edge: a good rim-light tool (keep for rims, vary width).
- day 7, 16:15: Day 7 16:15: falls streak pass — body hand, flat 7, length 40–110, fallwhite (+rim_warm near lip), noise-streak mask, NOT clipped, then vertical blend. Result: falls finally read as bright falling water in the whole view (good), but strokes overran the mask top and bottom by ~20 units (stubs above the brink, blunt ends in the pool). Lesson again: clip=true for any pass with a hard boundary. Repair: restate brink strip, foam over the bottom ends.
- day 7, 18:42: Day 7 18:42 — falls have degraded into a flat cloth sheet (trapezoid mask with straight sides/flat top, filled uniformly; graded noise pass + blends + streaks keep restating the trapezoid). Knife scrape over the foam left a weave crosshatch. New plan: lift the falls+foam with dipped rags, repaint dark wet rock, then build the water as 4 separate strands (own hand-drawn masks: convex glassy top bending over the lip, ragged widening body, white broken lower part), dark rock between them, then mist/foam with soft lost edges.
- day 8, 00:41: ## End of sitting 1 — handoff (day 8, 00:41)
  State: whole picture laid; most paint open or setting (pool and middle open; parts of background, canopy and birches setting/tacky; birch bases dry). Value chain now connects in squint: glow → lip → four strands → foam/mist → pale reflection column in pool. Darkest darks sit beside the falls.

  Open passages:
  - Birches (x~760–960, full height): still the lightest, crispest values and full-white faces; once dry, glaze the faces down a step (warm gray, medium ~0.75) leaving a thin glow-side rim; soften where they cross the haze; vary lenticel marks.
  - Boulder row (y 680–930 both banks): nine similar rounded "loaves" with uniform olive tops in two rows; vary size/overlap, break silhouettes, add facets and a near-plane mossy rock lower left overlapping the pool (critic's suggestion).
  - Falls (x 366–604, y 660–905): strands read as falling water at full view but sides are straight panels and the lip is a flat yellow band; ragged edges, glassy convex lip, fewer equal widths.
  - Shoulders beside the falls (x~290–340 and 664–712, y 610–700): soft brown blobs from a repair; restate as rock/undergrowth with rim light.
  - Pool (y 906–1250): reflections soft and plausible; needs crisper ripple lines in the foreground, better birch reflections, and the stepped waterline (bank toes at different heights).
  - Canopy (top third): inner edge still partly a continuous scallop; a few more sky holes and lost edges; right mass is heavy and uniform.
  - Signature not yet placed.

  Practical lessons (this easel, this canvas):
  - PALETTE LIMIT 16: scrape before knifing; palette{scrape={pileVar}} takes pile variables only. A pile scraped and then referenced in work() is re-knifed and needs a free slot.
  - clip=true on every body/flat pass bounded by a hard line (waterline, curtain, brink). Unclipped strokes overran by 20–70 units three times (pool over rocks, streaks above the brink, fan drags).
  - Never knife-scrape across passages to keep: scraping wet multi-layer paint leaves a weave crosshatch and scratches neighbours.
  - Dipped rag (w40, dip .9, p .85, 2 passes each direction, twice) lifts wet stacks to a stained ground; then repaint dark body cov 4. Rag faces fill fast on thick paint: take fresh rags.
  - Falls recipe F (lip lipglass → thinwhite veil (white 8, ochre .2, cobalt .1, thinner .5) flat 8 ×3 passes → fan 10–14 drags fallwhite load .3, pressure .55→.1 → one vertical blend → bright fan drags + pointed round accents), each pass clipped to the strand's own hand-drawn mask = reads as water. Repeated blends turn it to gray cloth; stop after one or two.
  - Graded `piles` by a distance function from the glow (glow/haze/amber/deeprust/woods) + vertical blend = the best large-mass method here (background, notch, glow zone repairs).
  - Noise-mask passes: always print mask:area() and look with mask= before painting (failed 117k "far trees").
  - Foliage clumps: hand-drawn soft outlines, lit side by projecting onto the glow direction, orangeleaf/leafrust/leafshade + lit dabs + rim silhouettes, then a blend = good canopy masses.
  - Rim light: knife held with blade ALONG an edge (angle = edge direction), moved 2–3 units across, load .35, pressure .12–.2 = thin broken bright line.
  Hypotheses (untested in isolation): blend over setting paint barely moves it; glaze over tacky birch paint may lift.
- day 9, 01:34: FAILED (day 9 01:34): glaze hand with lenticel pile (bone black+umber, no medium) over WET bank foliage = opaque dark horizontal slugs. Glaze needs medium (~0.75) and a dry underlayer; never glaze straight tube darks into wet paint.
- day 28, 06:33: Day 28 (sitting 1 continued): foreground mossy rock lower left (hand-drawn top line, knife rims, leaves); bank undergrowth restated as 25 hand-drawn foliage clumps graded lit→shadow toward the water; falls rebuilt as 4 strands with own masks (recipe F per strand, clipped) + convex glassy lip band + foam heads; floating leaves in eddies; ripple lines. Waited to day 28 so everything dried, then glazed birch shadow sides: barkglaze (raw umber 1, smalt .6, medium .6), glaze hand, filbert 12 soft, angle -pi/2, over DRY birch paint, then one blend — lowered the faces a step and kept a lit rim (medium .8–.9 was invisible; medium .45 streaky). Signed lower right (rigger, lenticel) — "mch"-like monogram.
  Glaze trial (scratch 12, dry white bars on dry amber): medium .8/.9 umber+smalt = invisible; medium .6 = visible warm-gray step; one blend after smooths the glaze-stroke ends.
- day 28, 06:33: Critic (day 28): not done. Falls read as a weir/curtain: level brink, box tops with tick fringe, rectangular rock, parallel even dark gaps to the foam, plumb outer sides, bright top/dull bottom, three cotton-ball foam domes. Fix: brink at ≥3 heights, jagged unequal rock crests, glassy convex lip band without ticks, gaps closing at different heights (narrow one ~760, middle ~800, left one a widening rock wedge crossed once by a veil), flare outer edges, brightest broken white low (820–880) + spray rising with lost edges, foam one low irregular mass threaded along the waterline. Then: foreground rock needs facets/moss/rim/wet band; break the symmetric loaves; birch bases pasted (sock/orange rectangle) + pale halo; ripples like stitches; glow keyhole edge hard (lose it at x520–700, y120–420).
- day 28, 21:21: Day 28 21:21 FAILED: mask(function) for "above the lips" returned 1 for every y>=560 outside the lip x-ranges → painted background tan into the pool as vertical orange bars and left a flat tan box above the falls. Lesson: every branch of a mask function must bound y (and x); print area and look with mask= before painting.
- day 29, 07:20: FAILED (day 29 07:20): blend over newFalls:grow(14) × lower zone mixed white water with the dark rock and small boulders inside the grown mask → a flat gray trapezoid box at the falls' feet. Lesson: a blend mask must not include neighbours of very different value; blend only inside the passage (shrunk), never a grown mask across a value edge.
- day 29, 07:56: FAILED (day 29 07:56): nx(i,t,y) for y>904 returns garbage (no strand rows there → lerp(1000,0,t)), so fan strokes ending at WL=906 crossed into X loops; the rock-repaint rect(330..650, 815..906) also covered the small boulders 6 and 8 with flat brown. Fix: clamp y≤900 in nx; subtract bmasks from repaint zones. Repair plan: dipped-rag lift of the open zone (dry paint beneath), then repaint carefully.
- day 29, 13:03: FAILED (day 29 13:03): pool repair in rect(190..810, 906..1096) — wrote a fade() but never used it; mix (waterdark+brushdark+amber) gave olive-brown → a big rectangle in the pool. Rule now: no rect-bounded repaints in continuous passages. Repaint the whole passage with soft-weighted piles to its natural edges (waterline, rocks, canvas edges).
- day 30, 04:52: FAILED (day 30 04:52): scumble hand with thinwhite (thinner .5) over OPEN wet foam/falls → opaque blocky white dabs with crackled dark marks (exactly the techniques-note warning: scumble wants a DRY underlayer). Do not scumble into wet paint.
- day 89, 07:16: ## End of sitting (day 89, 07:16) — handoff
  Since the critic's second visit: rebuilt the falls on a dark wet rock face with jagged pillar crests at different heights (lips at y 656/664/671/678), four strands with own masks, a merged lower curtain (lowerC) with a narrow rock wedge (wedgeL), foam as one low mass; replaced the canopy's hard keyhole with a hand-drawn soft window + a lit/shadow foliage band; restated the right bank undergrowth so birch feet sit inside it; gave the foreground rock a new broken silhouette, facets, moss cap, leaves, knife rims and a wet water edge; lowered the right loaf's top (breaks the symmetry); repainted the pool as one passage (poolPiles()). Everything older is dry; the two dark rocks at the falls' feet (x 290–384 and 596–694, y 830–912) and the foam strip are freshly open.

  Open passages:
  - Falls foot rocks (x 290–384 and 596–694, y 830–912): two near-identical dark rounded lumps bracketing the foam; vary their shapes/heights, add a facet and a rim, let foam overlap one.
  - Falls (x 345–630, y 640–905): the pillar tips read as fence posts and the lip caps as rounded boxes; when dry, glaze/scumble (over dry only) to break the caps, add spray/mist rising with lost edges, darken the lower curtain's middle so the white sits on top.
  - Upper slot above the brink (x 380–600, y 600–660): flat tan; needs a hint of upper stream surface/far bank tone so the water comes from somewhere.
  - Pool (y 906–1250): ripples are few now; add fine far ripples near the falls, longer sparse near ones; birch reflections pale and broken; light wedge in the foreground still slightly too yellow.
  - Left bank (x 0–280, y 340–700): big soft brown mass, less articulated than the right; a few lit leaf clusters on its crest facing the glow.
  - Canopy (top third): fine; maybe a few more sky holes on the right mass.

  Lessons added this sitting:
  - Scumble/glaze ONLY over dry paint. Scumble hand into wet foam = blocky crackled dabs; glaze of lenticel (no medium) into wet foliage = opaque slugs.
  - Never blend a grown mask across a value edge (white water + dark rock → gray box). Blend inside the passage, shrunk.
  - No rectangle-bounded repaints of continuous passages (pool rectangle). Repaint to natural edges with soft-weighted piles.
  - Every mask function must bound both x and y in all branches; print area and look with mask= before painting.
  - Helper nx(i,t,y) returns garbage beyond the strand's last row: clamp y.
  - Barkglaze (raw umber 1, smalt .6, medium .6) over dry birch white lowers the face a step; medium .8–.9 invisible.
  - Palette: 16 piles; scrape before mixing; a pile created as a local and lost cannot be scraped (keep piles in globals).
  - Waiting ~30 days of painting time dries nearly everything (thick foam took ~90).
- day 89, 10:29: Day 89 (sitting 3) — campaign 1, brink (critic's #1):
  - Scratch trial (dry tan bg + dry dark rock + dry white strands, ~40 d): horizontal flat-4 strokes, graded piles (haze+amber at the far edge → glow + a little fallwhite/foamsh toward the brink), clipped to a mask whose top fades over 6 units, then one horizontal blend = a believable thin stream surface. Ripple strokes of haze/amber round 1.6 = too busy at full detail; skipped on the painting.

- day 1, 09:00: ## Sitting 1 — plan
  Concept 4: autumn woodland stream falling over mossy rocks, small waterfall, white birches, gold/rust foliage reflected in pool.
  Canvas: 480 mm wide, aspect 0.8 (W 1000, H 1250), linen 18x15, ground lead white 10 + yellow ochre 0.4 + raw umber 0.15, 120 µm knife, texture 0.25 (warm cream).
  Composition (portrait): glow in the back woods upper left-center (~x380,y300), canopy gold/rust across the top with sky gaps; ledge ~y585 across middle; falls x~400–560 dropping to ~y780 in two strands split by a rock; pool y 780–1250 with vertical reflections of canopy and birches, foam at base; two birches on right bank (x~760, ~870), a slimmer one left behind the rocks; mossy rock lower left foreground, floating leaves.
  Values: lights = falls, foam, birches, glow; darks = rock under the lip, pool depths near banks, deep woods at edges; mids = foliage, moss.
  Method (wet-on-wet): a thin oily wet film first, then back to front, dark before light, all into open paint within the day: glow/back woods → canopy masses → rocks/ledge (knife) → pool base + vertical reflection pulls + horizontal passes → falls pulled down + foam → birches (thick light over wet dark) → moss lights, leaves, twigs, highlights.
  Palette: lead white; gold = chrome yellow + ochre (+white); rust = red earth + ochre + touch vermilion; darks = Prussian + red earth + umber; moss = green earth + chrome + ochre, Prussian + chrome + ochre; water = white + cobalt; birch shadow = white + smalt + umber.
- day 1, 09:00: Scratch trials 1 (dry cream ground, all into open paint, day 1 morning):

- day 239, 23:31: Day 239 — birch lenticels: scratch trial (dry trunks, 120 d): covering every other lenticel with birch_mid flat-6 strokes reads OK on the scratch, where the trunk was flat white; on the painting the bark is a streaky, glazed, multi-tone white, and the cover strokes read as smooth pale labels (value 132 vs streaked bark). Lifted (12-wide dipped rags, clean over dry). ACCEPTED as they are: at viewing distance the marks read as birch bark and their regularity is a close-up fault only. Lesson: a cover patch on a textured, glazed passage needs the same texture and glaze, not just its color; the scratch trial must reproduce the substrate's texture.
- day 240, 00:50: Day 240 — small repairs at full view: left foot rock's pale "helmet" cap and its orange left side covered with body dark (lent/rock), leaving a small lit plane (rock+haze+amber) at its top-left; the foreground rock's crenellated moss/dark boundary (picket line) repainted as a band graded mossdeep→rock→lent following the top contour (flat 7, angle along the contour, + blend) → now a soft turn from lit cap into shadow; the left bank toe extended to x 292 with a lobed soft outline to cover the vertical seam at x 318 (blend over dry seam did nothing; repainting with an irregular outline did).

  - Foam (scratch first, on a dry foam slab beside dry gray-tan water — the right substrate this time): gD2 glaze ribbons over white = barely visible even ×2 (glaze can't break a white edge). What worked: OPAQUE thin body ribbons over dry — "bites" of pool-water color (w1 = haze .62 + waterdark .28 + amber .10, value ~154 = matches the pool) cutting up into the foam's bottom band, "tongues" of foamsh/fallwhite running out below the edge, and drift ribbons (fp = foamsh .75 + haze .25, fading into w1) widening apart down to y~1010. Reads as soft dark seating. The gray label at x 250–283 covered with rock body.

Far edge level now; the trapezoid top shows as a faint plateau line (y~634) — acceptable at full view, check fresh.
- day 330, 02:16: ## End of sitting (day 330, 02:16) — handoff

  State: everything dry. This sitting I took up the critic's campaigns in order: (1) the brink: a stream surface with a level far edge running down to one continuous brink line, two bank toes, squared caps, lowered jambs; (2) the foot rocks: left tall/angular, right low half-drowned slab out at y~948; barcode dashes covered; (3) the pool: two gD2 glaze films grayed the glow reflection a step, and tapered wavy glaze ribbons (dark over light, light over dark) lay the water flat; (4) after the critic's third visit: foam broken into floating trails, rock seats glazed, stream toned down. Tried and lifted (failed): mist veil, opaque slab reflection, clumps over the loaves, re-cut left loaf, lenticel variation, spray puff.

  Accepted, with reasons (off the list):
  - Mid-ground loaves: quiet, low in value, read as mossy banks at full view; three tries to articulate them made them louder.
  - Birch lenticels: regular only up close; cover patches looked like labels on the glazed, streaky bark.
  - Left bank: the quiet shadow side against the busy right (critic agrees).
  - Canopy, glow, ghost trunks: leave.
  - Mist above the foam: none. A veil over dark rock became a cartoon cloud and over white was invisible; the broken foam and low whites carry the spray.
  - Falls caps: as they are (critic agrees).

  Open passages:
  - Stream above the brink (x 384–598, y 630–668): restated at the end of this sitting; at fresh eye, check whether the faint plateau top at y~634 reads as a line. If it does, lose it with one band of the background mix (haze/amber/deeprust) over dry; otherwise accept.
  - Foam trails (x 330–620, y 900–1010): restated at the end of this sitting; confirm at fresh eye that they read as foam lying on water, not as stripes.

  Practical lessons that still apply:
  - Everything wet laid over DRY paint lifts clean with dipped rags (dip 1.0, pressure 1.0, w 14–24, 2–3 passes each way, fresh rags often). That makes trial-on-the-painting cheap: lay it, look, lift it if it fails.
  - Glazes: gD2 (raw umber 1, smalt .8, lead white .3, red earth .2, medium .82) over dry = a gentle grayed step down. Never blend a glaze over dry paint (it streaks or crackles). A glaze ignores a mask's soft grading (the whole mask gets one film); grade with nested threshold masks. A glaze can't break a white edge; use opaque thin body ribbons of the neighbouring colour for that.
  - Tapered wavy ribbons (width = sin^0.5 taper, a gentle wave, gaps widening downward) are the mark that reads as water here: as glaze for ripples, and as opaque body for foam bites, tongues and drift.
  - Masks built from per-x noise at high frequency make combs and teeth. Use low-frequency noise for ragged edges.
  - Judge a trial on the real substrate, including its texture and its neighbours (white beside dark). Patches on a streaky, glazed passage read as labels.
  - Small single gestures (cracks, ledge lines, glints) over large dark masses read as drawn lines, not form. Form here comes from a few large graded planes.
  - clip=true for any pass bounded by a hard line; print mask:area() and look with mask= before painting; every branch of a mask function bounds x and y.
  - Palette: 16 piles. Some globals (nearbank, lenticel) point to different piles than the heaps on the board; use lent for the black-umber dark. Scrape by the variables that work.
- day 330, 02:47: Day 330 (sitting 4) — fresh-eye check and critic's campaign on the falls' outline:
  - Open passage, stream above the brink: up close (2.4×) the y~634 top shows as a faint pale mesa; at full view it reads as the far stream surface in haze, not a line. ACCEPTED (critic agrees; that area has been repainted enough).
  - Open passage, foam trails: at full view they read as foam drifting on the water, not stripes; up close a bit lacy. ACCEPTED.
  - Falls outline (critic): sides were one closed hard white-on-black line (plumb x~365–385 left, ~600–612 right). Scratch trial first (dry streaked white curtain beside dry rock dark, 60 d): (a) flat-4 dry-brush dark drags down the edge = soft gray smudges, edge stays straight (no); (b) "wedge" ribbons — pointed top inside the sheet, widening down and running out past the edge, roughen(1.2, 22), body round 3 rock/lent cov 3, clip, fill = clean dark gaps that read as fraying (good); (c) fan 11 drags of fallwhite, load .07–.15, pressure .25–.4→.03, starting 1–6 inside the edge and veering out 3–15 units (more lower down) = thin wispy threads; widens the curtain (good, keep few).
    On the painting: edges measured per y from lowerC+newFalls (eL/eR tables); 5 wedges left (y 722–822), 6 right (712–850), minus the foot rocks; then 7 threads left, 6 right, each clipped to a band of the edge (outer limit low-freq noise, widening down). The two lowest right wedges ate too much white (a dark notch at y 800–850): lifted with dipped 12-wide rags (dry beneath → clean). Then small tapered white tongues over the shoulders of both foot rocks (fallwhite/foamsh, round 3, clip). Edges view: the single plumb line is broken into a fray from y~720 down; the top 40 units stay crisp. Full view: the sheet widens and frays as it falls. Slot V left as is.
  - Ghost trunk at x~255–268 (critic's extra): scratch trial over a dry fartrunk pole on haze: scumble nested = blotchy; glaze (medium .6) nested = hazy but green-gray; body flat 4 vertical with load graded by y (bg mix glow .6/haze 1.1/amber .25) = the trunk dissolves downward (good). On the painting the first pass was lighter than the field (204 vs 196) → pale column; lifted with dipped rags; redone with amber graded up toward the bank (.2→.5), a second lighter pass higher (y 340–470) and one vertical blend inside. Now the trunk comes down out of the foliage and fades into the haze halfway to the bank. Still wet (open).
- day 370, 04:30: Day 370 — critic's 4th visit (asked): falls sides read as water now; trunk accepted; both open passages accepted. Remaining: (1) right-side threads at x 615–640, y 790–850 = a rake, and three tongues over the right foot rock = teeth; (2) foreground rock lower left = a smooth dome with an even moss horseshoe band and beaded leaves, the biggest "loaf"; (3) optional: even white ripple marks on the dark left water.

Result: right edge irregular; the two remaining tongues kept. Accepted.
  - Foreground rock (all over dry, so it would lift if it failed): new silhouette fgRock3 = old + a shoulder, top flatter to x~224, then a corner and a steep side. One body pass over the whole rock (flat 8, cov 4, clip): moss (mossdeep + a little mosslit3 at the very top) only inside a wandering depth mw(x) from the top (≈36 at the left, narrowing to 0 at x~245, low-freq noise), below it rock + lent + a little waterdark; stroke angle follows the top contour near the top and turns vertical lower down and on the steep side; one blend at angle .15. Then a warm rim: 7 knife segments of rim_warm along the measured top edge, x 112–238 only, blended once along the edge (they had read as a dotted line of beads) → a soft lit lip. Two leaves only, close together at x~140–158. Reads now as one large dark boulder with a mossy top turning into shadow, no ring.
  - Left water glints: mix for the pool's dark water = waterdark .8 / haze .14 / amber .06 (dry 91,88,81 on scratch; the pool around is 83–87). Three glints covered with round-3 body ribbons, clip, measured per point with probe (y 975.5, 992.8, 1040–1043); cover reads as faint ghost bands up close, invisible at full view. Remaining glints fewer and uneven.
- day 445, 04:49: Day 415–445 — closing work:
  - FAILED, lifted: a "bounce" band of lighter water-colored rock paint up the foreground rock's steep right side (to lose the edge against the water) = a separate pasted panel with a hard inner seam and a flat top. Lifted with dipped rags (dry beneath, clean; only a faint trace). Scratch test of lose() with water mix / mid mix on that edge (dry rock beside dry water) = a hairy frayed edge up close, barely different at viewing distance. Not applied: at full view the rock's right edge already meets the water quietly (rock 56 vs water 95, edges view blue/soft), so I accept it.
  - FAILED, lifted: warm glaze (yellow ochre 1, red earth .4, raw umber .15, medium .8) over the top 90 units of the faded ghost trunk, clipped to its width (scratch: warm tan, no halo when clipped) = on the painting olive-yellow and darker (149 vs 162). Lifted back to ~157 (a trace of film stayed, dried). The trunk stays as it was: a faint cool shaft fading into the haze. Accepted (critic called the warming optional).
  - Lesson confirmed: a glaze over a narrow cool-gray mark on a warm field shifts toward olive, not tan; scratch fields made of a fresh pole on fresh haze don't reproduce a mark that was faded with body paint and blended.
- day 445, 04:49: ## End of sitting 4 (day 445) — handoff

  State: everything dry. This sitting: at fresh eye I accepted both open passages. Then I took up the critic's campaign on the falls' outline: tapered dark wedges bite up into both outer edges from y~712 down, a few low-load fan threads veer out of the edges, and white tongues cross the shoulders of the foot rocks. The sheet now frays and widens as it falls, and the top 40–50 units under the lip stay crisp. I faded the thin ghost trunk into the haze with the background mix (body, load graded by height, blended). After the critic's fourth visit: broke the right-edge "rake" with one gap; re-shaped the foreground rock (flatter top to a corner, steep shadow side, moss as a wandering area that runs out at x~245, a soft warm lip toward the glow, two leaves); covered three of the even white glints on the dark left water with the water's own mix.

  Accepted, with reasons (off the list):
  - Stream above the brink: reads as the far water surface at full view; its faint plateau shows only at 2.4×. Repainted enough.
  - Foam trails: read as foam drifting on the water at full view; lacy only up close.
  - Ghost trunk (x~255): reads as a far trunk dissolving into the haze; a warming glaze turned it olive and was lifted.
  - Foreground rock's right edge against the water: quiet at full view; a lighter "bounce" band read as a pasted panel and was lifted.
  - Right foot rock's two small tongues and the left slot's V: read as water at full view.

  Open passages: none

  Practical lessons that still apply:
  - Wet over DRY lifts clean with dipped rags (dip 1.0, pressure 1.0, width 10–24, 2–3 passes each way, fresh rags often). Trial on the painting is cheap; once a mark has dried it can only be covered, so check marks while they're open.
  - To break a hard white edge: pointed "wedge" ribbons (top inside the sheet, widening down and out past the edge, roughen ~1.2/22) painted opaque with the neighbour's dark, clip, fill. Threads: fan 11, load .07–.15, pressure .3→.03, a few only, clipped to a band along the edge.
  - Cover patches must match the substrate's value and texture: mix for the pool's dark water = waterdark .8 / haze .14 / amber .06; measure the mark's exact position with probe first.
  - Glazes: gD2 over dry = gentle grayed step down; never blend a glaze over dry; a warm glaze over a cool gray mark goes olive.
  - Small single gestures over big dark masses read as drawn lines; form comes from a few large graded planes (the foreground rock: one body pass with piles weighted by depth from the top contour, stroke angle turning from along-contour to vertical).
  - clip=true for any pass bounded by a hard line; print mask:area() and look with mask= before painting; lose()'s where= must be a function or mask confined to the stretch you mean (a rect union gave rectangle outlines on scratch).
  - Palette: 16 piles; scrape before knifing new ones; use lent for the black-umber dark.

  Reflection: the falls became believable only when their silhouette stopped being a mask: the water frays where it is thinnest. The repeated lesson of this painting is that boundaries carry the reading: the waterline, the brink, the foam's bottom, the curtain's sides, the rock's moss band. Each read as fake while it was one even line, and each came alive when it was broken by the neighbour's own paint in tapered, unequal shapes. Next sitting: a look-only check of the whole canvas and a detail crop; if nothing new shows, the painting is finished.
- day 445, 05:04: Day 445 (sitting 5) — critic's campaign on the left mid-ground loaf (bm5, x 15–290, y 800–928):
  - Measured: water level at the left edge ~y 905–910 (value 67–70); the pool just below the old sag 70–73; the sag (below y 906) value 58–63, a convex dark underside down to ~928 at x 100.
  - Scratch (dry dark field + dry water field, 60 d): the critic's mix waterdark .8/haze .14/amber .06 dries to ~83–87 — too light for the pool under this rock (70). waterdark .87/deeprust .09/haze .02/amber .02 dried to 71. Used wC = waterdark .85/deeprust .11/haze .02/amber .02.
  - Painting: contact line level at y~906–908 (low-freq wobble, slight sag under the front bulge); sag mask = below contact × bm5 grown 5 − foot rock. One body pass flat 6, vertical, clipped → the sag was covered and the rock got a flat bottom. Then a reflection try: 64 flat-4 vertical pulls of rR (wC .7/rock .2/waterdark .1) below the contact line + a vertical blend = a gray pale band with a ruler-straight top, a shelf under the rock. LIFTED with dipped rags (w16, 4 rags, both directions) while open — clean, back to the dry pool beneath (the sag cover lifted too).
  - Second try: the critic's exact method — only the old sag's rows covered by tapered horizontal ribbons of wC (round 3 body, clip, 5 rows y 914–928, gaps between segments) → the dark breaks into horizontal shreds below the waterline, reads as broken reflection. Wet now; wait to dry before the gD2 seat (glaze only over dry).
- day 525, 05:19: Day 485–525 — left loaf, continued:
  - After drying (40 d): the sag is gone; the loaf ends on a level contact line at y~906–908 with a thin lighter waterline under it and horizontal dark shreds of wC below (broken reflection). In mirror view and at full view it no longer reads as a lid hovering.
  - Seat (critic's step 2): SKIPPED. On scratch, one gD2 film over a mid rust field moved it only 128→126; over this pool's 70 it would be invisible, and if it took, it would rebuild a dark band under the rock (the old sag). The shreds already seat it.
  - Critic's step 3 (run it off the edge): done anyway, because the rock's rounded left end still read as a separate object in the 0–160 crop. Extension mask = from the rock's measured top (833 at x 20) continued out of the frame (~839 at x 0, low-freq wobble) down to the contact line, minus the rock shrunk 8. Piles weighted by depth from the top: xA moss (mossdeep .68/rock .2/amber .12, dried ~89 on scratch) in the top ~8 units, xB (mossdeep .42/deeprust .2/rock .3/amber .08) under it, xC (rock .48/waterdark .3/deeprust .12/lent .1, ~63) for the body; flat 5, angle along the top turning vertical lower, clip. Only dark over red-brown, so no bank paint to match. Reads now as the toe of the left bank, matching the right loaf that runs off the right edge. Faint trace of the old rounded end inside, visible only at 2.4×.
  - Two dark tabs on the top edge (116,804; 228,808): covered with small hump masks of xA (round 3, clip) → small moss bumps in the lid; tiny at full view.
  - Orange smear right of the foreground rock (x 296–317, y 1158–1222, value 96 vs water ~94 but red): (1) two gD2 films = barely changed (96→99, slightly lighter/grayer) → lifted; (2) opaque cover q4 (waterdark .68/haze .16/amber .12/deeprust .04; scratch q2 dried 95) flat 4 vertical, edge soft = a gray-green ghost blob with its own edge (a label) → lifted with dipped rags (clean, faint trace). ACCEPTED: at full view it reads as a warm reflection of the rust bank beside the rock; it's the only warm note on that side of the rock, and repairs made it louder.
  - Mix lesson: the critic's dark-water mix (waterdark .8/haze .14/amber .06) dries to ~83–87 on scratch, too light for the water under the left bank (70). For the dark pool right under the banks: waterdark .85/deeprust .11/haze .02/amber .02 (dries ~71).
- day 565, 05:37: Day 525–565 — critic's 5th visit (asked): the left rock sits in the water now; the edge extension made it the toe of the left bank, balancing the right loaf; the seat was rightly skipped; the orange smear accepted. Optional: the comb of vertical olive drips under the mid-ground caps (picket line), largest on the left one; use the day-370 method once, stop rule: lift and sign off if it doesn't read.

content.text: Sitting 6: I took up your birch campaign. I used four nested glaze films per trunk instead of three: raw umber 1, smalt .6, medium .75. On scratch, medium .6 mottled over dry birch white, and .75 gave a smooth, even film. The films are clipped to each trunk's silhouette and their bottoms are low-frequency noisy and slanted. Bottoms are staggered: trunk A at y 52/128/246/388, trunk B at 30/96/282/418. The two long films leave a 3-unit lit rim on the glow side. Measured dry: A's lit face at y 140 went from 220 to 173, A's top averages 137, B's top 116, and the canopy around is ~100–114. Below the canopy the trunks are untouched (~177). I didn't add the canopy clump over the right trunk, because the glaze seemed enough. Please judge at full view whether the birches now sit in the canopy's shade, and whether anything else keeps the picture from being finished.

- Done on the left loaf only (over dry, so it would lift): loafM = bm5 + the extension − the foot rock; top contour measured every 2 units (topAt); zone = from the top down 66±5 (low-freq). One body pass, flat 8, cov 4, clip=loafM: xA moss in a band of wandering depth 7→13 units (narrower on the left/shadow side, low-freq noise), then xB, then xC + a little xC everywhere in the moss; stroke angle along the contour near the top, turning vertical ~20–30 units down; one blend (combZ shrunk 3) at angle .15. Dry after 40 d.

At full view it reads as the shadowed bank toe and breaks the row of three matching caps. At 1.9× it is smoother than its neighbours (a slightly airbrushed mound): ACCEPTED, because it sits on the shadow side and is quiet at full view.
- day 565, 05:37: ## End of sitting 5 (day 565) — handoff

  State: everything dry. This sitting was the critic's left-rock campaign. The sag below the waterline is covered with tapered horizontal ribbons of dark water, so the rock now meets a level contact line with broken dark shreds below it. The rock runs off the left edge as the toe of the bank. The two tabs on its top are covered with moss. After the critic's 5th visit I replaced the comb of olive drips under its cap with one graded body pass, a narrow dull moss band turning into shadow. Tried and lifted: vertical reflection pulls under the rock (a gray shelf), a gD2 glaze and then an opaque cover on the orange smear beside the foreground rock (the cover left a gray label).

  Accepted, with reasons (off the list):
  - The orange smear right of the foreground rock: at full view it reads as the rust bank reflected beside the rock; repairs made it louder (the critic agrees).
  - The seat glaze under the left rock: skipped; over 70-value water it barely registers and would rebuild the dark band.
  - The left loaf's smooth graded surface: quiet on the shadow side at full view.
  - The right two mid-ground caps' combs: smaller; left as they are (the critic suggested the left one only).

  Open passages: none

  Practical lessons that still apply:
  - Wet over DRY lifts clean with dipped rags (dip 1.0, pressure 1.0, width 12–24, 2–3 passes each way, fresh rags). Trial on the painting is cheap; judge marks while open.
  - Measure before mixing: the pool under the left bank is ~70; waterdark .85/deeprust .11/haze .02/amber .02 dries ~71. The critic's waterdark .8/haze .14/amber .06 dries ~85 (right for the mid pool, too light at the bank).
  - Tapered horizontal ribbons of the water's own dark (round 3 body, clip) turn an object's dark that runs below the waterline into broken reflection; vertical pulls there make a shelf.
  - gD2 over dry barely moves a mid or dark passage (128→126); it only works over light fields.
  - Opaque cover patches on a streaked, warm passage read as labels unless they reproduce the texture; accept small warm notes that read at full view.
  - Moss caps: one body pass with piles weighted by depth from the measured top contour, stroke angle along the contour turning vertical, one low-angle blend. That replaces combs and horseshoes.
  - Palette: 16 piles; some globals (lenticel, nearbank, glow) don't point to the heaps on the board. Scrape the piles you just made (they work) to free slots.

  Reflection: the last two critiques were about seating. Objects float when their dark keeps going past the line where they meet something, and they sit once the dark is cut at a level line and broken into the neighbour's marks. Running the rock off the frame made it part of the land, not an object. Next sitting: a look-only check of the whole canvas and a detail crop. If nothing new shows, the painting is finished.
- day 605, 05:42: Day 565–605 (sitting 6) — critic's campaign: the upper birches inside the canopy.
  - Measured first (probe, dry): lit face of A at the top ~220 (point), 153 averaged across the trunk incl. lenticels/shade; B top ~137 avg; canopy around 98–114. Masks mA/mB still exist (global); widths per y measured from them.
  - Scratch 1 (dry birch white on dry rust, 60 d, flat test bars): barkglaze (raw umber 1, smalt .6, medium .6) ×3 nested = 219→153 at the top, but the films on the scratch looked mottled/bruised with crackle-like grain; red-earth variant warmer but not better; medium .7 ×3 = 167. medium .75 ×5 nested = 151 top, 159, 186, 199 down the steps — cleanest, smoothest film.
  - Scratch 2 (proper birch trunks with lenticels, dry 60 d): bark75 ×4 nested films with LOW-FREQ NOISY, SLANTED bottoms, clipped to the trunk = a continuous darkening upward, no visible rings, dried 177 (top) → 190 → 215 (untouched). Turps-thinned umber/smalt and an opaque birch_shade body/scumble were tried too: body cover flattens the bark texture (a smooth label), scumble patchy. Glaze kept the bark marks.
  - Painting: bark75 (raw umber 1, smalt .6, medium .75), glaze hand, filbert 12 (A) / 9 (B), angle -pi/2, clip to the trunk shrunk 1.5/1.2. Four nested films per trunk, bottoms staggered between trunks: A at y 52/128/246/388, B at 30/96/282/418 (noise amp 4–6, slope ±.25–.35). Films 1–2 (the long ones) leave a 3-unit lit rim on the glow (left) side; films 3–4 cover the full width at the top.
  - Result (dry, 40 d): A's lit face at y 140: 220→173; A top avg 137, B top avg 116, A at 250–370 ~142; below the canopy untouched (177). Colour warm gray, not olive. At 1:1 the steps don't show; no halo. Full view and squint: the birches now dim into the canopy shade and are brightest where they stand against the haze; the falls own the white again. Edges view: birch outlines in the canopy now dim, broken orange, no longer the longest hard lines.
  - The optional canopy clump over the right trunk: NOT done; the glaze was enough, and clump-over-object tries on this canvas (loaves) made louder objects.
  - Lesson: medium .75 is the sweet spot for this umber/smalt glaze over dry birch white (.6 mottles, .8–.9 vanishes); four films with noisy slanted bottoms grade a trunk without rings.
- day 645, 07:38: Day 605–645 (sitting 6, cont.) — critic's visit after the glaze: "value done, space not yet: the trunks' edges are still the hardest lines in the top half and nothing crosses them; also the birch reflections start right under the right loaf."

     - Measured the canopy right of each trunk: A side 103–116 (rust-orange 160,98,51), B side 91–99 (darker rust).

- day 645, 07:38: ## End of sitting 6 (day 645) — handoff

  State: everything dry. This sitting was the critic's birch campaign:
  (1) Four nested glaze films per trunk of bark75 (raw umber 1, smalt .6, medium .75), clipped to each trunk, with staggered noisy, slanted bottoms. They dim the upper birches inside the canopy (A's lit face 220→173, tops 116–137) and keep a 3-unit lit rim on the glow side. The falls own the white again.
  (2) After the critic's visit: soft lobed ribbons of the canopy's own rust bite into each trunk's shadow-side edge in three staggered stretches, and one canopy lobe crosses each trunk where the canopy ends. The birches now go behind the lowest leaves and come out lit into the haze.
  Tried and lifted: five ways of making the birch reflections start lower (gD2 films, horizontal dark ribbons, low-load fade pulls, a white-free glaze, opaque fork shapes).

  Accepted, with reasons (off the list):
  - Birch reflections under the right loaf: they read as the trunks' reflections at full view, quieter than the gold column. Every cover over the soft dry streaks made a louder shape (curtains, icicles, blotches, ladders).
  - A's crossing lobe: a little band-like at 1:1, but it joins the canopy edge on both sides and reads as leaves at full view.
  - The optional canopy clump at the top of the right trunk: not needed.

  Open passages: none

  Practical lessons that still apply:
  - Wet over DRY lifts clean with dipped rags (dip 1.0, pressure 1.0, width 12–16, 2 passes each way, 4–6 fresh rags; blot isolated specks with a 6-wide rag). Trial on the painting is cheap; judge it while open.
  - Umber/smalt glaze over dry birch white: medium .75 is the clean film (.6 mottles, .8–.9 vanish). Grade with 3–4 nested films whose bottoms are low-frequency noisy and slanted, clipped to the object. Then no rings show.
  - To lose an object's edge into foliage: outline{char="soft", lobe 4–5} through tapered points along the measured edge, painted with short round-3 body strokes (angle jitter), clip, in the neighbour's measured mix. Plain tapered polys painted flat make crisp stripes.
  - gD2 contains white: over dark water it veils (lighter). A glaze keeps the contrast ratio, so it can dim a light but not remove it. Opaque covers of soft blended lights over dry always get their own edge.
  - Measure mixes on scratch and dry them before use: deeprust .55/leafrust .25/orangeleaf .1/amber .1 ≈ 111; deeprust .85/leafrust .15 ≈ 99 (rust canopy); waterdark .85/deeprust .11/haze .02/amber .02 ≈ 71 (pool under the banks).
  - clip=true for passages with hard bounds; print mask:area() and look with mask= before painting; low-frequency noise for ragged edges.
  - Palette: 16 piles. Scrape the piles just made to free slots (gD2, leafrust and orangeleaf were scraped this sitting; bark75, wgM and deeprust are on the board).

  Reflection: the critic was right that value alone doesn't place a thing in space. The glazed trunks were dimmer but still lay on the canopy like tape until leaves passed in front of them and their shadow edge dissolved into the foliage. Overlap and lost edges did what the value step couldn't. The reflections taught the opposite lesson: an error that is soft and blended into a dry passage is cheaper to accept than to fix. Next sitting: a look-only check of the whole canvas and a detail crop. If nothing new shows, the painting is finished.

content.text:
Yes, the birches now sit in the canopy's shade. In the full view and in squint they dim as they go up into the leaves and are brightest where they stand clear against the haze, so the falls have the white to themselves again. The rust lobes biting into their shadow edges did the rest: in the edges view the trunks' outlines inside the canopy are broken and dim instead of running unbroken top to bottom.

What the picture does well, it now does throughout. In squint, the light is one vertical chain: glow, then brink, then curtain, then foam, then the gold column in the pool. The dark banks frame it, with light only on their crests, which commits the picture to backlight. The hardest edges and the strongest value contrast are on the falls and nowhere else. The things you fought over the longest now read as what they are at full view: the frayed sides of the curtain, the foam lying broken on the water, the rocks seated at a level waterline, the left loaf running off the edge as the toe of the bank.

I looked for a change that matters and didn't find one I'd make. The one thing I noticed is the two orange leaf collars where the canopy crosses the trunks. They sit at almost the same height, so they read a little alike. But your own reflections lesson applies here: a small, quiet error on a dry passage is cheaper to accept than to fix.

The painting is finished. In the next sitting, don't make any marks. End it by looking at the whole canvas and one detail crop in normal color, then sign off.
